title: Chemicals, PPE and exposure prevention
audience: Trainee or new worker on the pressure cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Interpret safety data sheets, prevent incompatible chemical use, assess aerosols and ensure suitable eye, hearing and skin protection.

instruction.heading: Read the label and the safety data sheet
instruction.body: A cleaning product is a hazardous chemical until its label and its safety data sheet say otherwise. The label tells you the product's intended uses, its dilution, the contact time and the first steps for exposure. The safety data sheet gives more detail, including hazards, protection, handling, storage, spill response and disposal. Safe Work Australia's guidance says a copy of the safety data sheet for each chemical in use must be kept in the hazardous chemical register, and must be easy to access for every worker who uses, handles or stores the chemical, and for anyone else who may be exposed to it. The same guidance says the information in a safety data sheet is general, so the worker must work out what applies to the site. Before a product is used, read its label and the current safety data sheet, and confirm the uses and incompatibilities the sheet names.

instruction.heading: Incompatible chemicals and mixing
instruction.body: Some chemicals must not be mixed or stored together, because a reaction can produce heat, gas or a more hazardous product. Safe Work Australia's storage guidance says that incompatible chemicals should be kept apart and stored well away from each other, and that some hazardous chemicals are not compatible with one another. The working rule is to use one product at a time, as its label directs, and to rinse equipment between products only where the label allows it. Do not combine products to make a stronger solution. Do not use a decanted liquid when its origin, concentration and contents are unknown. Do not combine an acid-based product with a chlorine-based product, and check each safety data sheet.

instruction.heading: Aerosols, overspray and exposure
instruction.body: Pressure work turns liquid into a fine spray and an aerosol. The spray can carry product onto skin, eyes, clothing and nearby vehicles, and it can be breathed in. Control the spray first. Lower the spray where the product allows it, position the operator so the spray does not drift toward people, and stop when wind carries the spray toward them. Personal protective equipment supports those controls, but it does not make an unsafe spray method acceptable. The WorkSafe Victoria alert says anyone near jetting operations should wear eye protection, and that the operator controlling the water flow should wear at least safety glasses and a face shield.

instruction.heading: Selecting PPE for eyes, hearing and skin
instruction.body: Select PPE after the task assessment, not before it. For eyes, the alert's minimum for the operator, and eye protection for anyone close to the spray, form the baseline. For hearing, the Safe Work Australia standard is 85 decibels as an average over an eight-hour day, and hearing protection is needed where noise cannot be controlled by other means. Where a worker frequently wears hearing protection to stay below the standard, audiometric testing must be provided. For skin, select gloves that the safety data sheet names as suitable for the product, and wear waterproof clothing where the product or the spray will reach the body. Gloves that are not suitable for a product can fail without warning. Wash facilities and a place to change out of contaminated clothing are part of the control, not an extra.

instruction.heading: Spills, runoff and storage
instruction.body: Check the spill response in the safety data sheet before use, and keep a spill kit suited to the product. Do not wash a chemical or its wastewater into a stormwater drain. The Victorian EPA guide on stormwater pollution, dated August 2007, says the runoff of wastewater and liquid or solid waste into the stormwater system must be avoided. Store products in their original labelled containers, in a suitable container for each product, and keep them apart from anything they are incompatible with.

instruction.heading: Competency boundary
instruction.body: This lesson gives the basic approach to chemicals, PPE and exposure. It does not give authority to use a restricted or high-hazard chemical, to remediate contamination, or to carry out work that needs a licence or a training competency. Refer those tasks to the supervisor and to a specialist, and record the referral.

procedure: Identify each product by its name on the label, and read the label for uses, dilution, contact time and first steps.
Obtain the current safety data sheet, and confirm the stated uses, incompatibilities, first aid and spill response.
Confirm that no two products will be combined, and that no decanted or unlabelled liquid will be used.

Select PPE from the task assessment: eye and face protection, hearing protection where noise cannot be controlled, gloves and clothing suited to the product, and respiratory protection where the safety data sheet requires it.
Assess the spray and aerosol risk, set the spray direction and position, and stop if wind carries spray toward people or vehicles.
Check the spill kit, the waste route and the wash facilities before the product is opened.
Store the product in its labelled container, apart from any incompatible product, and record its use on the job record.

workedExamples.situation: A worker is offered an unlabelled bottle described as a powerful mould remover for a brick walkway. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: Decline its use until the product's identity and its safety data sheet are verified. An unlabelled product cannot be assessed for hazards, incompatibilities or disposal. Tell the supervisor, and assess whether the treatment is in scope at all. Mould and biological contamination are dealt with in a separate lesson, and any such task is referred to a specialist. Record the decision and the client communication about the substitution.

workedExamples.situation: Two products are on the truck: one chlorine-based and one acid-based, and a job sheet asks for both on the same surface. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the two be used together to save time?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Do not combine them, and do not apply one straight after the other without the safety data sheets confirming that this is allowed. Read each safety data sheet for incompatibilities. Record the decision. Keep them apart and refer the sequence to the supervisor.

workedExamples.situation: During a wash, a gust carries spray across a neighbour's car and onto a person standing near the fence. This is an example job.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the spray, move the person clear, and reposition the operator so the spray goes away from people and property. PPE does not fix this, because the spray should not reach the person in the first place. Reassess the wind and the spray method before resuming, and record the event and the owner's notification.

equipmentAndPpe: Product labels and current safety data sheets, kept with the job record
Eye protection and a face shield for the operator, and eye protection for anyone near the spray
Hearing protection where noise cannot be controlled by other means
Gloves and waterproof clothing suited to the product, as named on the safety data sheet
Respiratory protection where the safety data sheet requires it.
Spill kit suited to the product, and a container for the waste
Wash facilities and a clean place to change

commonErrors.error: Reading only the label and not the safety data sheet.
commonErrors.prevention: Read the label and the current safety data sheet, and confirm the uses and incompatibilities before use.

commonErrors.error: Mixing two products to get a stronger result.
commonErrors.prevention: Use one product at a time, as its label directs, and never combine products to make a stronger solution.

commonErrors.error: Using a decanted liquid of unknown origin.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only labelled products with a known identity, and refer any unknown liquid.

commonErrors.error: Skipping eye protection because the spray is only water, or treating PPE as the main control.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the spray control first, and then the eye protection the alert describes.

commonErrors.error: Washing chemicals or wastewater into a stormwater drain.
commonErrors.prevention: Contain the wastewater and dispose of it by the route the safety data sheet and local rules set.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Safety data sheets: keep a current copy for each product, in the hazardous chemical register, and make it easy to access for workers and others who may be exposed.
Storage: incompatible chemicals are kept apart and stored well away from each other, and containers must suit the chemical.
Eye and face protection: the WorkSafe Victoria alert sets out the minimum for the operator and the eye protection for anyone near the spray.
Noise: the exposure standard is 85 decibels as an average over eight hours, with audiometric testing where protection is worn frequently above it.
Stormwater: the 2007 Victorian EPA guide says wastewater and liquid waste must not run into the stormwater system.
Completing this lesson does not give authority to use restricted chemicals, remediate contamination, or carry out work that needs a licence or competency.

qualityStandard: Product identity, concentration, contact time, storage and spill response are checked against the label and the current safety data sheet.
The stated uses and incompatibilities are confirmed, and no two products are combined.
Eye, hearing, skin and respiratory protection, where required, is selected from the task assessment and the safety data sheet.
No unknown decanted liquid is used, and wastewater is not released to stormwater.
documentationEvidence: Product record with name, label, safety data sheet reference and date
PPE selection record with the reason for each item
Spray and wind check record, with the stop decision if one was made
Spill kit check and waste disposal record
Storage record showing products kept apart from incompatible products
summary: Read the label and the current safety data sheet before use, and confirm the uses and incompatibilities they name.
Keep products apart, never combine them, and never use an unknown decanted liquid.
Control the spray first, then select the eye, hearing, skin and respiratory protection the task needs.
Keep wastewater out of stormwater, and refer any task that needs a licence or a specialist.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must be verified before a cleaning product is used?
options: A decanted liquid of unknown origin is used for a stronger result on the surface, since the label was too worn to read
The label and current safety data sheet are read, the uses and incompatibilities are confirmed, and PPE is chosen from a task assessment
Two products are combined so the job takes less time and the surface is done sooner, which the client prefers and pays for
Eye protection is skipped, since the spray is only water and does not reach the face of the worker at any distance

knowledgeChecks.question: Overspray is reaching a neighbour's car during a gust. What is correct?
options: Worker PPE is enough, so the work can continue while the car is parked there
Stop, reposition the spray away from people and property, and reassess before resuming
Increase the pressure to clear the area faster before the wind gets worse
Ask the neighbour to move the car while the work continues around them and the crew

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the Safe Work Australia storage guidance say about incompatible chemicals?
options: Store them together to save space in the store room today
Keep incompatible chemicals apart, stored well away from each other
Mixing is allowed if the label says so on the bottle itself
Only the supplier decides how they are stored on the site
